hidden_target.material_initial_state: Equimolar 99.5%-pure W, Mo, Ta, Nb, and V elemental powders, mechanically alloyed and granulated, together with a polished TC4 (Ti6Al4V) substrate measuring 50 × 20 × 10 mm.
hidden_target.intervention: WNbMoTaV spherical RHEA powder was produced by ball milling, spray granulation with 2.5 wt.% starch at 40 wt.% solids, and 35 kW radiofrequency-plasma spheronization under Ar/H2 (70/6 L·min−1). A 2 mm-thick preset powder layer was then laser clad onto TC4 while varying laser power from 3.1 to 3.9 kW; coatings made at 3.3, 3.5, and 3.7 kW were analyzed in detail because the 3.1 and 3.9 kW coatings had poorer quality.
hidden_target.conditions: Laser cladding used a 5 mm spot, 600 mm·min−1 scanning speed, 20 mm defocus, and 99.99% He shielding at 15 L·min−1. Wear was tested by linear reciprocation against a 4 mm Si3N4 ball under 20 N, with a 2 mm wear track, 1 Hz frequency, and 30 min duration. Vickers microhardness was measured on coating cross-sections at 0.98 N with a 10 s dwell.
hidden_target.structural_mediator: Dense, metallurgically bonded coatings primarily containing a high-strength BCC solid solution plus a Ti-rich phase, with rapid-solidification grain refinement. Increasing power reduced unfused powder and grain size but increased substrate dilution and Ti-rich-phase formation; 3.5 kW provided the best balance, whereas 3.3 kW retained more unfused powder and 3.7 kW caused over-burning and greater Ti-rich substrate dilution.
hidden_target.mechanism: Lattice distortion in the BCC solid solution, solid-solution strengthening, fine-grain/grain-boundary strengthening, and high resistance to plastic deformation increased hardness and limited plowing during wear. Too little laser power caused incomplete melting, defects, organizational inhomogeneity, and lower crystallinity; excessive power caused over-burning, stronger Marangoni-driven Ti diffusion, higher dilution by the softer substrate phase, and reduced support from the BCC structure. Oxide formation during sliding also produced a partly protective tribo-oxide layer.
hidden_target.predicted_outcome: Relative to uncoated TC4, WNbMoTaV laser-clad coatings are expected to increase surface microhardness and wear resistance, with a nonmonotonic dependence on laser power and an optimum near 3.5 kW.
hidden_target.baseline: Bare TC4 (Ti6Al4V) substrate tested under the same microhardness and Si3N4-ball reciprocating-wear conditions; its average hardness was 341.25 HV0.3 and wear-volume loss was 6.09 × 10^7 μm3.
hidden_target.boundary: The reported performance trend applies to the successfully formed 3.3, 3.5, and 3.7 kW coatings under the stated cladding and wear-test conditions. The 3.1 and 3.9 kW coatings were judged poorer and were excluded from subsequent detailed analysis; behavior outside the tested power range was not established.
hidden_target.discriminating_measurement: Cross-sectional Vickers microhardness and reciprocating wear measurements, including coefficient of friction, 3D-profiler wear volume and scar depth, and calculated wear resistance, were used to compare the coatings with TC4. XRD, SEM, and EDS identified phase structure, grain size, unfused powder, dilution, morphology, elemental segregation, and wear mechanisms.
hidden_target.actual_result: The 3.3, 3.5, and 3.7 kW coatings had average hardnesses of 586.71, 670.67, and 601.22 HV0.3, respectively—1.72, 1.97, and 1.76 times the TC4 value. Their wear-volume losses were 3.28 × 10^7, 1.75 × 10^7, and 2.85 × 10^7 μm3, corresponding to wear resistances 1.83, 3.42, and 2.13 times that of TC4. Maximum wear-scar depths fell from about 34.4 μm for TC4 to 18.3, 7.7, and 13.3 μm. Thus, 3.5 kW gave the highest hardness, lowest wear, and lowest stable average friction coefficient (about 0.40). Coating wear was mainly oxidative, slight abrasive, and adhesive wear, whereas TC4 underwent more severe abrasive, adhesive, and oxidative wear.
